title: Services, JPA Repositories, and PostgreSQL
summary: Map PostgreSQL tables to JPA entities, query them through Spring Data repositories, and keep business rules and transactions in services.
intro: Behind every endpoint is a service that applies the business rules and a repository that reads and writes PostgreSQL. This is where the bugs that cost money live: stock sold twice, totals that drift, pages that run a query per row. In this lesson you follow shopfront's checkout from the table to the transaction, and see the SQL that Hibernate really runs.

steps.title: Tables first, then entities
steps.body:
In a team, the schema lives in version control as SQL migrations. Flyway runs each `V<n>__<name>.sql` file in `db/migration` once, in version order, when the app starts, and records it in the `flyway_schema_history` table. To change the schema, you add the next file. You never edit one that already ran, because every other database has already applied it.

An entity is a class that maps one table: `@Entity` on the class, `@Id` on the key, and one field per column. Spring Boot maps a field like `priceCents` to the column `price_cents` for you. With `ddl-auto: validate`, Hibernate compares the entities with the tables at startup and stops the app when they disagree, so a missing migration fails right away instead of on the first query.

JPA needs a constructor with no arguments, but it can be `protected`. Give the entity a real constructor and methods that keep its data valid, instead of a setter for every field.

examples.title: The catalog tables
examples.prompt: The migration that creates the categories and products tables.
examples.code:
-- The catalog: categories, and the products in them. Prices are whole cents.
CREATE TABLE categories (
    id   bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    slug text NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (slug ~ '^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$')
);

CREATE TABLE products (
    id          bigint GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    sku         text    NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (sku ~ '^[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{3}$'),
    name        text    NOT NULL,
    description text    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    price_cents bigint  NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents > 0),
    stock       integer NOT NULL,
    active      boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
    category_id bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES categories (id),
    -- JPA's @Version column: every update checks it and adds one.
    version     bigint  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
examples.explanation: Constraints are the last line of defense: `UNIQUE` on `sku`, a `CHECK` on its format and on the price, and a foreign key to `categories`. The Java code checks the same things, but a constraint also stops a bad row that comes from a script, a bug, or two requests racing. Money is whole cents in a `bigint`, never a floating point type, so sums never pick up rounding errors. `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` lets PostgreSQL number the rows, and `version` is there for the entity's optimistic locking.

examples.title: The Product entity
examples.prompt: The class that maps the products table. Stock only changes through methods that keep it valid.
examples.explanation: `GenerationType.IDENTITY` matches the identity column, so PostgreSQL assigns the id on insert. `@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)` loads the category only when something asks for it. The default for a to-one relation is eager, which quietly adds a join or a query everywhere the entity is loaded. `@Version` turns on optimistic locking: every UPDATE says `where id=? and version=?` and adds one, so when two checkouts read the same stock, the second one to commit fails instead of selling the shop's last stand mixer twice. `removeStock` throws a 409 `ConflictException` rather than let stock go below zero.

steps.title: Repositories write the queries
steps.body:
With Spring Data JPA you declare a repository as an interface, and Spring writes the class at startup. Extending `JpaRepository<Product, Long>` gives you `save`, `findById`, `findAll` with paging and sorting, `count`, and `delete`.

For anything else, name a method and Spring Data writes the query from the name: `findBySku`, `existsBySku`, `findBySkuIn`, `findByCustomerEmail`. A typo in a property name stops the app at startup, not in production. When a name would get too long, write the query in JPQL with `@Query`. JPQL uses entity and field names, not table and column names.

Then watch how many queries each request runs. Touching a lazy relation on every row of a list runs one more query per row. This is the N+1 problem, and it is one of the most common reasons a Spring API is slow. Fetch what the response needs up front, with `@EntityGraph` or `join fetch`. Turning on `spring.jpa.show-sql` while you develop prints every statement.

examples.title: Queries from method names
examples.prompt: Product lookups that Spring Data writes from their names. The output is the SQL one call to `findBySku` ran, with `spring.jpa.show-sql=true`.
examples.output: Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category_id,c1_0.id,c1_0.name,c1_0.slug,p1_0.description,p1_0.name,p1_0.price_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.stock,p1_0.version from products p1_0 join categories c1_0 on c1_0.id=p1_0.category_id where p1_0.sku=?
examples.explanation: `findBySku` returns an `Optional`, so each caller decides what a missing product means. `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "category")` adds the join you see in the SQL, so reading `product.getCategory()` afterwards runs no query. `findBySkuIn` loads every product of an order in one query with `IN`, instead of one query per line. Overriding `findAll(spec, pageable)` with the same entity graph keeps a page of the catalog at two queries, the page and its count, however many rows it shows.

examples.title: A query of your own
examples.prompt: Order lookups, and the one statement `findWithLinesById` ran for `GET /api/orders/4`.
examples.output: Hibernate: select o1_0.id,o1_0.cancelled_at,o1_0.currency,o1_0.customer_id,c1_0.id,c1_0.created_at,c1_0.email,c1_0.name,c1_0.password_hash,c1_0.role,l1_0.order_id,l1_0.id,l1_0.product_id,p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category_id,p1_0.description,p1_0.name,p1_0.price_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.stock,p1_0.version,l1_0.quantity,l1_0.unit_price_cents,o1_0.placed_at,o1_0.status,o1_0.subtotal_cents,o1_0.tax_cents,o1_0.tax_rate_basis_points,o1_0.total_cents from orders o1_0 join customers c1_0 on c1_0.id=o1_0.customer_id left join order_lines l1_0 on o1_0.id=l1_0.order_id left join products p1_0 on p1_0.id=l1_0.product_id where o1_0.id=? order by l1_0.id
examples.explanation: `findByCustomerEmail` follows a relation, `order.customer.email`, and takes a `Pageable`, so it returns one page plus the total count. `findWithLinesById` needs the order, its customer, its lines, and each line's product, so `join fetch` loads them all in a single statement. Without it, building the response would run one query for the lines and then one per line for its product. `left join fetch` keeps an order that has no lines, and the text block keeps the query readable.

steps.title: Services own rules and transactions
steps.body:
A service method is one business operation, and `@Transactional` makes it all or nothing. Spring opens a transaction before the method runs and commits it when the method returns. If the method throws an unchecked exception, everything it wrote rolls back.

Shopfront marks each service class `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` and each method that writes `@Transactional`. Every public method then runs in a transaction, reads skip the work of checking for changes, and the methods that write stand out in review.

Inside a transaction, the entities you load are managed: Hibernate remembers their state and writes every change at commit, with no `save` call. This is called dirty checking. Services also build their response records before they return, while the transaction is still open, because `spring.jpa.open-in-view: false` closes the database session before the JSON is written.

examples.title: Placing an order
examples.prompt: Checkout as one transaction, and what ana gets back for two copies of Dune and a headlamp.
examples.explanation: The method loads everything it needs in two queries, the customer and all the products, then checks each line. A SKU listed twice or not for sale is 422, and `removeStock` throws a 409 when there is not enough. If any line fails, the exception rolls back the whole transaction, including stock already taken for earlier lines. Prices come from the catalog, never from the client, and each line keeps a copy of its price, so a later price change never rewrites a past order. Money stays in whole cents from start to end.

examples.title: Cancelling without save
examples.prompt: Cancelling an order never calls `save`. The output is the SQL that ana's cancel request ran.
examples.output:
Hibernate: select o1_0.id,o1_0.cancelled_at,o1_0.currency,o1_0.customer_id,c1_0.id,c1_0.created_at,c1_0.email,c1_0.name,c1_0.password_hash,c1_0.role,l1_0.order_id,l1_0.id,l1_0.product_id,p1_0.id,p1_0.active,p1_0.category_id,p1_0.description,p1_0.name,p1_0.price_cents,p1_0.sku,p1_0.stock,p1_0.version,l1_0.quantity,l1_0.unit_price_cents,o1_0.placed_at,o1_0.status,o1_0.subtotal_cents,o1_0.tax_cents,o1_0.tax_rate_basis_points,o1_0.total_cents from orders o1_0 join customers c1_0 on c1_0.id=o1_0.customer_id left join order_lines l1_0 on o1_0.id=l1_0.order_id left join products p1_0 on p1_0.id=l1_0.product_id where o1_0.id=? order by l1_0.id
Hibernate: update products set active=?,category_id=?,description=?,name=?,price_cents=?,sku=?,stock=?,version=? where id=? and version=?
Hibernate: update orders set cancelled_at=?,currency=?,customer_id=?,placed_at=?,status=?,subtotal_cents=?,tax_cents=?,tax_rate_basis_points=?,total_cents=? where id=?
Hibernate: update products set active=?,category_id=?,description=?,name=?,price_cents=?,sku=?,stock=?,version=? where id=? and version=?
examples.explanation: `requireVisible` loads the order, its lines, and their products in one query, the first statement. `order.cancel` changes the order's status in memory, and `addStock` changes each product. At commit, Hibernate compares each managed entity with the state it loaded and writes the ones that changed: one UPDATE for the order and one for each product. Each product UPDATE checks and bumps `version`. If another request had changed that product in between, the UPDATE would match no row, and the whole cancel would roll back with a 409.

recap:
- Flyway migrations own the schema. Add a new `V<n>__` file for every change, and never edit one that ran.
- Entities map tables. Keep `ddl-auto: validate`, a protected no-argument constructor, lazy to-one relations, and `@Version` where updates can race.
- Repositories are interfaces. Name a method and Spring Data writes the query, or write JPQL with `@Query`.
- Fetch what a response needs up front with `@EntityGraph` or `join fetch`, so a page never runs one query per row.
- Put `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` on the service class and `@Transactional` on writes. An exception rolls everything back, and managed entities are saved at commit.
